The feeling of possibility

Some places make
your world bigger.

A quiet chair under an old tree. A conversation that stays with you. The first glimpse inside a laboratory, or a room full of books you want to read.

We want to bring that feeling to young people everywhere: beauty, belonging, and the sense that there is so much more to discover.

Around the Yard

Find your place.
Then find your people.

We’re imagining a shared campus that reaches beyond geography. Come with a question, an unfinished idea, or simply a little curiosity.

01 / Follow a question into a book

A good book makes your world a little bigger.

Choose a question that intrigues you. Read something worth your attention. Bring an idea to a small circle of readers, and discover what someone else noticed.

Imagine a conversation like this
“Which idea in this book changed your mind—and which one would you challenge?”

The practice: pay attention, form a view, and stay open to a better one.

The person comes before the possibility

Dream bigger.
Grow into it.

Ambition needs somewhere to take root. Our approach is built around the habits children can practice: asking better questions, knowing where they stand, learning from others, and returning to difficult things.

Meaningful work, thoughtful feedback, and people who help them see a little farther.

01See a bigger world.+

Encounter great ideas, unfamiliar fields, and people doing remarkable work. Let a new possibility become a goal that feels personally meaningful.

02Know where you are.+

Make a prediction. Try something. Notice the gap between what you expected and what happened. Honest reflection gives the next step a direction.

03Learn from excellence.+

Study a beautiful proof, a thoughtful argument, or an ingenious design. Compare approaches, ask what makes them work, and raise the standard of your own work.

04Keep finding a way.+

Return after a failed attempt. Change the strategy, ask for help, and make one concrete improvement. Give persistence a thoughtful practice.

05Grow with great people.+

Build relationships with mentors and peers who are curious about your thinking. Prepare questions, listen carefully, and put their feedback to work.

A rhythm of discovery

Big possibilities.
Small, meaningful steps.

A spark becomes a question. A question becomes a project. A little practice becomes something a young person can call their own.

01 / Discover

“What if…?”

A book, a conversation, or a glimpse inside a lab opens a door. Choose a question you want to follow.

02 / Practice

“Let me try.”

Set a small goal. Read, sketch, test, or build. Make an honest first attempt and see what you learn.

03 / Reflect

“Now I see.”

Talk it through with someone who helps you think. What worked? What surprised you? What needs another look?

04 / Grow

“What’s next?”

Use the feedback. Revise your work. Take on the next challenge with a little more understanding and independence.

A glimpse of the experience we’re building. Activities and mentor programs are in development.

Human connection. Thoughtful technology.

Keep the spark alive
between conversations.

We’re designing an AI-supported learning companion to help young people turn a mentor’s guidance into everyday practice: make a plan, work through a challenge, and prepare a better question.

Mentors bring judgment and perspective. Technology helps carry the learning forward. The goal is growing independence.

A founder’s starting point

Some places change
what you think is possible.

The idea began with professors who opened my mind—and the feeling of Harvard Yard. People reading under trees. Friends working on ideas. Beautiful surroundings that make you want to sit, think, and stay a little longer.

As a parent, I see what access to thoughtful mentors and a rich learning environment can mean for a child. I want more young people to have that experience, wherever they grow up.

I think of it as a nursery for the mind. A shared place for the books, relationships, surroundings, and everyday practices that help a person become.

A few things you might wonder

A little more
about the Yard.

Who is The Yard for?

We’re initially imagining curious young people around ages 11–16, including those still discovering what interests them. The starting point is willingness to explore, try, and learn with others.

Is this an online community or a physical place?

The vision begins with an online community: reading circles, mentor conversations, and meaningful projects that connect young people across geography. Local gatherings and visits to inspiring places are part of the longer-term ambition. The illustrated campus represents that vision.

Can my child join a program now?

The Yard is an early-stage venture. Programs, mentor participation, and pricing are still being developed. You can try the first-spark activity on this page today; it’s a self-guided sample, with no account or registration required.

What would parents see?

Our intention is to share concrete examples of learning: the goal a child chose, the work they attempted, and how they responded to feedback. Young people should have a meaningful say in their goals and room to develop independence.

Is The Yard part of Harvard or MIT?

The Yard is an independent venture. Harvard and MIT refer to the founder’s educational background. The Yard is not affiliated with or endorsed by either university.
